blockMcqs.question: Roughly how much slower is a DRAM miss than an L1 hit?
options: About 2x
About 10x
About 100x
About 10,000x
blockMcqs.explanation: L1 is ~1ns and DRAM ~100ns, so the gap is the cliff most code trips on.

blockMcqs.question: What does an out-of-order core guarantee about your results?
options: Instructions execute strictly in program order
Results are retired in program order
No two instructions ever overlap
Branches are never speculated
blockMcqs.explanation: It runs work as inputs are ready but retires in order, so output looks sequential.

blockMcqs.question: Why is summing values over a threshold faster on a sorted array?
options: Sorting reduces the number of additions
The branch becomes predictable, avoiding flushes
Sorted data fits entirely in L1
The compiler skips the comparison
blockMcqs.explanation: A predictable branch lets the predictor stop mispredicting and refilling the pipeline.

blockMcqs.question: When the CPU reads one int, what actually gets loaded?
options: Exactly that 4-byte int
The whole 64-byte cache line it sits on
The entire array
Nothing until the line is full
blockMcqs.explanation: Transfer happens per line, so ~16 neighboring ints come along for free.

blockMcqs.question: Why can a long dependency chain be slow with no cache misses?
options: Each step waits on the last, preventing overlap
Dependent instructions always miss cache
The branch predictor disables forwarding
Registers run out of space
blockMcqs.explanation: Serialized latency is exposed because the pipeline cannot overlap dependent work.

blockMcqs.question: Why do arrays often beat linked lists despite identical O(n)?
options: Arrays use fewer additions
Contiguity enables prefetching; lists chase scattered pointers
Linked lists recompute hashes each step
Arrays are stored in registers
blockMcqs.explanation: Array scans are bandwidth-bound; pointer-chasing is serialized and latency-bound.

blockMcqs.question: When does struct-of-arrays (SoA) layout pay off?
options: When loops touch only a few fields per record
When you always read whole records
When records have a single field
When data never fits in cache
blockMcqs.explanation: Contiguous per-field storage makes each cache line fully useful and vectorizes well.

blockMcqs.question: How do you fix false sharing between per-thread counters?
options: Use a single shared atomic counter
Pad each counter to its own cache line
Lower the table load factor
Disable the hardware prefetcher
blockMcqs.explanation: Separate lines stop the coherence ping-pong that invalidates other cores' copies.
